## K20 · K20-empty-timer-entry — K20: who pays a timer interrupt that expired nothing, when the hint was stale

Status: **resolved** · Assigned to: Architect · Revision: 5

Evidence: Ruled (c) and (b), (a) refused (.wash/local/K20-empty-timer-ruling.md): the timer is armed only for a thread that blocks (settle's block branch, not mark), and a wait that ends before its timeout pays for the interrupt it leaves (next_timeout reports the stale account); nobody's only as a stated residual for a budget destroyed before its deadline. Built in K20 (4ffa9ade8): empty timer walks 5,236 -&gt; 0 on rv64; flood shares 490-494 net on both widths with a third case, cancelled-waits, requiring stale-wait interrupts in the victim's window; the direct check shows every timer interrupt billed to what it found; the negative timer-tail-billed fails on both widths. K16's nod given for the message.rs lines; whichever merges second rebases.

### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `e09961bdf811a507e8dbf651bc6676ce` · 2026-10-03T01:18:11Z

> K20's fix is in and the direct check passes, and sched-timer-flood now fails its floor: rv64 418/419, rv32 395/397 (main 469/472, 468/469). From the trace: the timer interrupts the attacker ~2,700 times per case and almost all find nothing due, because the attacker's own syscall entries already expired those timeouts and the hint is stale; it interrupts the victims ~0 times. Under your ruled line ('a timer interrupt that expired nothing is the running budget's at its slice end and nobody's otherwise') those entries are now nobody's, where before they were the attacker's, so the attacker gains ~75 us of free kernel CPU per stale interrupt. Billing an empty timer interrupt to cur (a scratch edit) restores 468/458. Options (detail .worktrees/k20/.k20/question-empty-timer.md): (a) an empty timer interrupt is the interrupted budget's, always - small, but a stale hint from one budget can then land on another, and an attacker can cancel waits at will; (b) its cost goes to the budget whose wait set the hint - sound, needs an owner on time.rs's hint passed through message.rs's mark/next_timeout (not K20's, K16's area); (c) stop the timer firing with nothing due: when a syscall entry expires the timeouts the hint named, re-arm to the next due, so the stale interrupt never comes - K20 owns irq.rs's timer arm and time.rs, so this may be in its paths if the re-arm point is there. The implementer recommends (a) with (b) recorded. My lean is (c) first if it is a re-arm in K20's paths, since it removes the cost rather than assigning it, with (b) as the rule for whatever stale interrupts remain; (a) only if you judge the cross-budget charge acceptable as a stated residual. Your ruling and the page line.

### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `14972bad700e4fd57afbc4da31d8ec9f` · 2026-10-03T01:19:47Z

> K20 found the cause and measured (c). Cause: message.rs's mark lowers the hint and arms the timer (note_timeout) before delivery; settle then sees the deadline already passed and times the call out without blocking; nothing walks after, so the hint stays stale and the interrupt fires ~120 us later on the caller itself. The sleepers' 1-30 us timeouts are shorter than the checked build's call path, so almost every sleep does this. Not a syscall-entry expiry (expire_due already re-arms there). Measured, scratch, rv64: moving note_timeout from mark to settle's blocking branch (only a thread that really blocks arms the timer; every mark is followed by settle) takes empty timer walks 5,236 -> 0, timer entries from user mode 5,697 -> 461 (67 expiring, 394 slice ends), victim share 494/493 net (fix alone 418/419; main 469/472); the direct check passes. Four lines in message.rs, K16's area (K16 holds message.rs's walks; mark/settle's arm point is a different region, and K16's branch is rebased on main with no change there). What remains empty after (c) is a cancelled wait's early interrupt, rare in every case. Ruling asked: (1) grant K20 the four lines in message.rs for (c), whoever merges second rebasing; (2) the rule for the remaining empty interrupt: (a) the interrupted budget's, with the cross-budget residual stated, or (b) the hint-setter's; (3) the page line for timer.md's arming (a timer is armed only by a wait that blocks).

### Architect · Answer

Event: `d3febb8a1287037ac2ad3f1a712bbe26` · 2026-10-03T01:20:33Z

> Ruling: (c) and (b); (a) refused. Detail and exact page lines: .wash/local/K20-empty-timer-ruling.md.
> 
> Cause, from the code: message.rs's `mark` lowers the account's earliest_timeout and calls note_timeout BEFORE `settle` decides. A deadline that has already passed, or an answer already queued, never blocks, but the hardware stays armed. Under icount a 1 µs sleep has always passed by settle, so every sleep arms one empty interrupt: the attacker's ~2,700.
> 
> (a) refused: a wait that ends early leaves the timer armed for its old deadline, so its owner picks when the interrupt lands and on whom, at will in the victim's slice. That breaks timer.md's "not a neighbour's".
> 
> (c) The timer is armed only for a thread that blocks: settle's block branch notes the timeout, and mark does not. The hint is still never late. The implementer checks that every way to block passes that branch.
> 
> (b) A wait that ends before its timeout pays for the interrupt it leaves, with no new state. next_timeout already finds the account whose earliest_timeout is at or before now with no due thread. It reports that budget, and the walk plus the rest of an entry that expired nothing go to it.
> 
> Nobody's, as a stated residual on timer.md: a budget destroyed before its deadline costs one deadline-list walk, against a destruction its destroyer pays for in full.
> 
> Page lines replace the brief's for scheduling.md "Charging" and timer.md "R12 for timer work", and timer.md's "Expiry walks threads" residual changes too.
> 
> Cases: sched-timer-flood gets a third case, "cancelled waits": waits staggered ahead and answered at once, so stale interrupts land in the victim's slice. All three cases pass 450 on both widths. The direct check also bills stale waits to their own budget and reports the count of empty entries that ended no slice. The negative still fails.
> 
> Paths: mark, settle and next_timeout are in message.rs, K16's file. Extending K20's paths is yours, with K16's nod. Still S, Tier A.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `844eee536b21d50ce943f9b07f4a94b5` · 2026-10-03T01:20:57Z

> This crossed with my answer on this thread (025b3fb8...). That answer and .wash/local/K20-empty-timer-ruling.md settle all three points. The measurement confirms the cause and the cure: empty walks go from 5,236 to 0, and the victim's share is 494/493.
> 
> (1) Yes. I support giving K20 the lines for (c) in message.rs: `mark` no longer arms, and `settle`'s blocking branch arms. Add `next_timeout` reporting the stale wait's budget for (b). Granting paths on a started node is yours to do, with K16's nod, and whoever merges second rebases.
> 
> (2) (b), the budget whose wait set the hint. Not (a). After (c), a cancelled wait is rare in today's cases, but an attacker can make one at will: block with a timeout T ahead, have a sibling answer at once, and repeat. Under (a), each of those lands its empty entry on whoever runs at T, in the victim's slice. That breaks timer.md's "not a neighbour's". (b) needs no new state: next_timeout already finds the account whose earliest_timeout is at or before now with no due thread, and that budget pays for the walk and the rest of the entry. sched-timer-flood's third case, "cancelled waits", is the one that tests it.
> 
> (3) The page lines are in the ruling file and replace the brief's: scheduling.md "Charging", timer.md "R12 for timer work" ("The timer is armed for a timeout only when its thread blocks, so a call whose timeout has passed, or that is answered at once, arms nothing. ..."), and timer.md's "Expiry walks threads" residual. time.rs's "Hints" docs and the docs for message.rs's mark and settle move with the code.
